# What's Across (whatsacross.com)

> Click any coastline on a 3D globe and see which country lies across the water in every direction. Every compass bearing (sampled each 0.25°, or 0.1° in high detail - 1,440 or 3,600 directions) is followed along a great circle to its first landfall. Free, runs entirely in the browser, no account, no adverts. Formerly nearest.land.

What's Across answers "what's across the ocean from me?" properly: not due east or west, but along great circles, which is why parts of the US east coast face Australia and Land's End faces Brazil. Pick a point on any coast (or use your device location) and you get a north-up polar chart of 1° wedges coloured by the country you would reach in that direction, blank where land is in view, plus a list clockwise from north with bearing ranges and the nearest distance to each country. The paths are drawn on the globe, and the antipode of the chosen point is marked and named.

Method: Natural Earth 1:10m country polygons (public domain) are rasterised in the browser to a ~10 km grid; the chosen point is snapped to the water's edge; each bearing is walked along its great circle until the first land cell, continuing past the antipode if needed. Land within about 20 km counts as "land in view". Bearings are sampled every 0.25° (1,440 bearings); on the sphere neighbouring bearings are about 20 km apart at 5,000 km and at most 28 km apart (a quarter of the way round the world), closing again towards the antipode, so a distant island narrower than that can fall between bearings. The 0.1° setting brings the gap down to at most about 11 km, roughly one cell of the ~10 km grid. Results are inherently approximate (see the coastline paradox: the finer a coast is measured, the longer it gets).

Daily puzzle: one mystery shore per UTC day (same for everyone, seeded from the date); guess it from its view in six tries, share an emoji result.
Map layers: Political (per-country colours), Terrain (Natural Earth I shaded relief) and Satellite (NASA Blue Marble imagery) - cosmetic only, the analysis is identical on all three.
Three modes: Coast (default) snaps the pick to the water's edge and follows each direction across the sea to its first landfall; Anywhere starts from the exact point, on land or at sea, and follows each direction to the first land that is not the country you are standing in (from Berlin, east is Poland at about 80 km); Over land is the same but never crosses water.

Technical: static site, three.js, MIT licensed, installable PWA that works offline once loaded. No tracking scripts, no backend.

## Links

- [Globe](https://whatsacross.com/): the app
- [What's directly across the ocean](https://whatsacross.com/across/): static answers for 37 well-known coastlines (New York, Ocean City, Miami, San Francisco, Lisbon, Land's End, Cape Town, Mumbai, Tokyo, Sydney, Perth and more) - due north/east/south/west, the widest parts of each sea view, the furthest country and each place's antipode, computed with the globe's own engine, plus the sea and land records
- [Shared view](https://whatsacross.com/?at=50.14,-5.41): `?at=lat,lon` opens the page with that coastline already picked (this example is Land's End); `#at=lat,lon` works too. A view picked from the device's own location is never written to the address bar, and sharing it gives only the area, rounded to about 10 km, in a `#at=` fragment

## Related

- [orrery.live](https://orrery.live/): interactive 3D solar system by the same author
- [weathermodels.app](https://weathermodels.app/): the "Weather here" button opens the forecast for the picked point on that separate site (nine models compared); from the device's own location it passes only the area, rounded to about 10 km
- [Scan the Horizon](https://scanthehorizon.app/): names the hills, mountains, towns and islands on your horizon, with their distances, by the same author
- [Adam's Arcade](https://games.adamwoodland.com/): all of the author's free browser games and tools
- [Adam Woodland](https://adamwoodland.com/): the author, an OT/ICS cybersecurity consultant; this site is a side project
